solution:
In Stock notation the Roman numeral gives the oxidation number of the metal, so Mercury(II) means \(\mathrm{Hg}\) is \(+2\), and chloride is \(\mathrm{Cl^{\ominus}}\), i.e. \(-1\).

For the compound to be neutral the oxidation numbers must sum to zero, so two chloride ions are needed for one mercury :

\((+2) + 2(-1) = 0\)

Formula : \(\mathrm{HgCl_2}\)

Thallium(I) means \(\mathrm{Tl}\) is \(+1\), and the sulphate ion is \(\mathrm{SO_4^{2\ominus}}\), i.e. \(-2\).

For the compound to be neutral, two thallium(I) ions are needed for one sulphate ion :

\(2(+1) + (-2) = 0\)

Formula : \(\mathrm{Tl_2SO_4}\)

Tin(IV) means \(\mathrm{Sn}\) is \(+4\), and oxide is \(\mathrm{O^{2\ominus}}\), i.e. \(-2\).

For the compound to be neutral, two oxide ions are needed for one tin :

\((+4) + 2(-2) = 0\)

Formula : \(\mathrm{SnO_2}\)

Chromium(III) means \(\mathrm{Cr}\) is \(+3\), and oxide is \(\mathrm{O^{2\ominus}}\), i.e. \(-2\).

The smallest whole numbers that make the total zero are two chromium and three oxygen :

\(2(+3) + 3(-2) = 6 - 6 = 0\)

Formula : \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_3}\)

The **combustion of methane** — the reaction this chapter's own opening "Can you recall" box asks you to write — takes carbon from \(-4\) to \(+4\).

\(\mathrm{CH_4(g) + 2O_2(g) \longrightarrow CO_2(g) + 2H_2O}(l)\)

**Carbon in \(\mathrm{CH_4}\).** H bonded to a non-metal is \(+1\), and the molecule is neutral :

\(x + 4(+1) = 0\), so \(x = -4\)

**Carbon in \(\mathrm{CO_2}\).** O is \(-2\), and the molecule is neutral :

\(x + 2(-2) = 0\), so \(x = +4\)

So the oxidation number of carbon rises by 8 units, from \(-4\) to \(+4\) — carbon is oxidised, and oxygen (from \(0\) in \(\mathrm{O_2}\) to \(-2\)) is reduced, so this is a redox reaction.

The equation is balanced : 1 C, 4 H and 4 O on each side.

Nitrogen goes from \(-3\) to \(+5\) when **ammonia is oxidised to nitric acid** :

\(\mathrm{NH_3(g) + 2O_2(g) \longrightarrow HNO_3(aq) + H_2O}(l)\)

**Nitrogen in \(\mathrm{NH_3}\).** H bonded to a non-metal is \(+1\), and the molecule is neutral :

\(x + 3(+1) = 0\), so \(x = -3\)

**Nitrogen in \(\mathrm{HNO_3}\).** H is \(+1\), O is \(-2\), and the molecule is neutral :

\((+1) + x + 3(-2) = 0\), so \(x = +5\)

Nitrogen therefore rises by 8 units, from \(-3\) to \(+5\), and oxygen falls from \(0\) to \(-2\), so the reaction is redox.

The equation is balanced : 1 N, 3 H and 4 O on each side.

[Note: this chapter does not print a reaction taking nitrogen all the way to \(+5\). Its own worked Problem 6.6, \(\mathrm{3CuO + 2NH_3 \longrightarrow 3Cu + N_2 + 3H_2O}\), takes nitrogen only from \(-3\) to \(0\). The reaction above is supplied to satisfy the question; both oxidation numbers in it are derived from the chapter's own rules 3, 4 and 6.]

Throughout, H bonded to a non-metal is \(+1\), O is \(-2\), an alkali metal is \(+1\), the sum for a neutral molecule is 0 and the sum for a polyatomic ion is its charge.

**a. \(\mathrm{H_2\underline{S}O_4}\)** : \(2(+1) + x + 4(-2) = 0\), so \(x = +6\).

**b. \(\mathrm{H\underline{N}O_3}\)** : \((+1) + x + 3(-2) = 0\), so \(x = +5\).

**c. \(\mathrm{H_3\underline{P}O_3}\)** : \(3(+1) + x + 3(-2) = 0\), so \(x = +3\).

**d. \(\mathrm{K_2\underline{C}_2O_4}\)** : K is \(+1\), so \(2(+1) + 2x + 4(-2) = 0\), giving \(2x = +6\) and \(x = +3\).

**e. \(\mathrm{H_2\underline{S}_4O_6}\)** : \(2(+1) + 4x + 6(-2) = 0\), giving \(4x = +10\) and \(x = +\dfrac{5}{2} = +2.5\). This is one of the fractional, AVERAGE oxidation numbers described in the chapter's "Do you know?" box — in the tetrathionate ion two S atoms are at \(+5\) and two at \(0\), and \(10/4 = 2.5\).

**f. \(\underline{\mathrm{Cr}}_2\mathrm{O_7^{2-}}\)** : the sum equals the ionic charge, so \(2x + 7(-2) = -2\), giving \(2x = +12\) and \(x = +6\).

**g. \(\mathrm{NaH_2\underline{P}O_4}\)** : Na is \(+1\), so \((+1) + 2(+1) + x + 4(-2) = 0\), giving \(x = +5\).

[Textbook misprint: the instruction reads "Justify that the following reactions ARE redox reaction", but sub-item (b), \(\mathrm{HF(aq) + OH^{\ominus}(aq) \longrightarrow H_2O}(l) + \mathrm{F^{\ominus}(aq)}\), is NOT a redox reaction — H is \(+1\), O is \(-2\) and F is \(-1\) on both sides, so not one oxidation number changes and there is no oxidant and no reductant to identify. It is a neutralisation. Sub-items (a) and (c) are redox as the instruction claims. The item is preserved as printed and (b) is answered on its own terms below.]

A reaction is redox only if some element's oxidation number changes. Two of the three reactions below qualify; the third does not, and is treated on its own terms.

**a. \(\mathrm{2Cu_2O(s) + Cu_2S(s) \longrightarrow 6Cu(s) + SO_2(g)}\)** — this IS a redox reaction.

In \(\mathrm{Cu_2O}\), O is \(-2\), so each Cu is \(+1\). In \(\mathrm{Cu_2S}\), S is the more electronegative partner and is \(-2\), so each Cu is again \(+1\). On the right, Cu is free metal at \(0\), and in \(\mathrm{SO_2}\) sulphur is \(+4\).

- Reduced : Cu, from \(+1\) to \(0\) — six Cu atoms, gaining \(6 \times 1 = 6\) electrons.
- Oxidised : S, from \(-2\) to \(+4\) — one S atom, losing 6 electrons.

The electron count balances at 6 either way.

Oxidant : \(\mathrm{Cu_2O}\), whose copper is reduced. Reductant : \(\mathrm{Cu_2S}\), whose sulphur is oxidised. Note that \(\mathrm{Cu_2S}\) is doing both jobs at once — its sulphur is oxidised while its own copper is reduced — so \(\mathrm{Cu_2O}\) is the only purely oxidising reagent here.

**b. \(\mathrm{HF(aq) + OH^{\ominus}(aq) \longrightarrow H_2O}(l) + \mathrm{F^{\ominus}(aq)}\)** — this is NOT a redox reaction.

H is \(+1\) in \(\mathrm{HF}\), in \(\mathrm{OH^{\ominus}}\) and in \(\mathrm{H_2O}\). O is \(-2\) in \(\mathrm{OH^{\ominus}}\) and in \(\mathrm{H_2O}\). F is \(-1\) in \(\mathrm{HF}\) and \(-1\) as \(\mathrm{F^{\ominus}}\).

Not one oxidation number changes, so there is no oxidation, no reduction, no oxidant and no reductant. It is a neutralisation — a proton transfer from the acid \(\mathrm{HF}\) to the base \(\mathrm{OH^{\ominus}}\).

**c. \(\mathrm{I_2(aq) + 2S_2O_3^{2\ominus}(aq) \longrightarrow S_4O_6^{2\ominus}(aq) + 2I^{\ominus}(aq)}\)** — this IS a redox reaction.

In \(\mathrm{S_2O_3^{2\ominus}}\) : \(2x + 3(-2) = -2\), so S is \(+2\). In \(\mathrm{S_4O_6^{2\ominus}}\) : \(4x + 6(-2) = -2\), so S is \(+\dfrac{5}{2}\) on average. Iodine goes from \(0\) in \(\mathrm{I_2}\) to \(-1\) in \(\mathrm{I^{\ominus}}\).

- Oxidised : S, from \(+2\) to \(+2.5\) — four S atoms, losing \(4 \times 0.5 = 2\) electrons.
- Reduced : I, from \(0\) to \(-1\) — two I atoms, gaining 2 electrons.

Oxidant : \(\mathrm{I_2}\). Reductant : \(\mathrm{S_2O_3^{2\ominus}}\) (thiosulphate).

[Textbook note (not an error): the item asks which ONE of the four pairs has its second species in the oxidised state, but TWO of them qualify — (a) \(\mathrm{Mg / Mg^{2\oplus}}\) and (b) \(\mathrm{Cu / Cu^{2\oplus}}\) are each a free metal beside its \(+2\) cation, so in both the second species is the oxidised form. Only (c) and (d), where the second species is an anion, are excluded. Both qualifying pairs are given below rather than choosing arbitrarily between them.]

**What is oxidation?** The chapter gives two equivalent definitions. In terms of oxidation number, oxidation is an **increase in the oxidation number** of an element in a given substance. In terms of electrons, it is the **loss of electrons** by a species. (Classically it was also described as combination with oxygen, or removal of hydrogen.)

**Which member of each pair is the oxidised form?** In every pair the first species is the free element, whose oxidation number is \(0\) by rule 1, and the second is an ion, whose oxidation number is its charge by rule 2. So compare the second against \(0\) :

| pair | second species | oxidation number | change from \(0\) |
|---|---|---|---|
| \(\mathrm{Mg / Mg^{2\oplus}}\) | \(\mathrm{Mg^{2\oplus}}\) | \(+2\) | increase — **oxidised** |
| \(\mathrm{Cu / Cu^{2\oplus}}\) | \(\mathrm{Cu^{2\oplus}}\) | \(+2\) | increase — **oxidised** |
| \(\mathrm{O_2 / O^{2\ominus}}\) | \(\mathrm{O^{2\ominus}}\) | \(-2\) | decrease — reduced |
| \(\mathrm{Cl_2 / Cl^{\ominus}}\) | \(\mathrm{Cl^{\ominus}}\) | \(-1\) | decrease — reduced |

So the species in its oxidised state is \(\mathrm{Mg^{2\oplus}}\) in (a) and \(\mathrm{Cu^{2\oplus}}\) in (b); in (c) and (d) the second species is the reduced form.

\(\mathrm{2Na(s) + S(s) \longrightarrow Na_2S(s)}\)

**Assign the oxidation numbers.** On the left both Na and S are free elements, so each is \(0\) by rule 1. On the right, sodium is an alkali metal and is \(+1\) in all its compounds (rule 2); the compound is neutral, so

\(2(+1) + x = 0\), giving \(x = -2\) for sulphur.

**Justification.**

- Na : \(0 \longrightarrow +1\), an increase, so sodium is **oxidised** (each Na loses 1 electron, 2 electrons in all).
- S : \(0 \longrightarrow -2\), a decrease, so sulphur is **reduced** (gaining 2 electrons).

One element's oxidation number increases while another's decreases, in the same reaction, and the 2 electrons lost equal the 2 gained. That is exactly the chapter's definition of a redox reaction.

**Oxidising agent : sulphur \(\mathrm{(S)}\)** — it brings about the oxidation of sodium and is itself reduced.

**Reducing agent : sodium \(\mathrm{(Na)}\)** — it brings about the reduction of sulphur and is itself oxidised.

In Stock notation the oxidation number of the metal is written as a Roman numeral in parentheses immediately after the metal's symbol, as in the chapter's own examples \(\mathrm{Au(I)Cl}\), \(\mathrm{Sn(IV)Cl_4}\) and \(\mathrm{Mn(IV)O_2}\). Take H as \(+1\), Cl as \(-1\) and O as \(-2\), and set the total for each neutral compound to zero.

| compound | working | metal O.N. | Stock notation |
|---|---|---|---|
| \(\mathrm{HAuCl_4}\) | \((+1) + x + 4(-1) = 0\) | \(+3\) | \(\mathrm{HAu(III)Cl_4}\) |
| \(\mathrm{Tl_2O}\) | \(2x + (-2) = 0\) | \(+1\) | \(\mathrm{Tl(I)_2O}\) |
| \(\mathrm{FeO}\) | \(x + (-2) = 0\) | \(+2\) | \(\mathrm{Fe(II)O}\) |
| \(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}\) | \(2x + 3(-2) = 0\) | \(+3\) | \(\mathrm{Fe(III)_2O_3}\) |
| \(\mathrm{MnO}\) | \(x + (-2) = 0\) | \(+2\) | \(\mathrm{Mn(II)O}\) |
| \(\mathrm{CuO}\) | \(x + (-2) = 0\) | \(+2\) | \(\mathrm{Cu(II)O}\) |

Note that \(\mathrm{FeO}\) and \(\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}\) are exactly the case Stock notation exists for : the same metal in two different oxidation states, which the names "iron oxide" alone could not distinguish.

**a. \(\mathrm{Cr(OH)_4^{\ominus}}\)**

H is \(+1\) and O is \(-2\), so each hydroxide group contributes \((-2) + (+1) = -1\). The species is an ion of charge \(-1\), so the sum of all oxidation numbers is \(-1\) :

\(x + 4(-1) = -1\), giving \(x = +3\).

So H \(= +1\), O \(= -2\), Cr \(= +3\).

**b. \(\mathrm{Na_2S_2O_3}\)**

Na is an alkali metal, \(+1\); O is \(-2\); the compound is neutral :

\(2(+1) + 2x + 3(-2) = 0\), giving \(2x = +4\) and \(x = +2\).

So Na \(= +1\), O \(= -2\), S \(= +2\). This \(+2\) is an AVERAGE over the two sulphur atoms, which by rule 8 need not be in the same state individually.

**c. \(\mathrm{H_3BO_3}\)**

H bonded to a non-metal is \(+1\); O is \(-2\); the molecule is neutral :

\(3(+1) + x + 3(-2) = 0\), giving \(x = +3\).

So H \(= +1\), O \(= -2\), B \(= +3\).

The chapter states the rule directly : the **more positive** the value of \(\mathrm{E^0}\), the stronger the redox couple is as an oxidising agent, because a more positive \(\mathrm{E^0}\) means a greater tendency to gain electrons.

**a.** \(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) has \(\mathrm{E^0} = 1.36\ \mathrm{V}\) and \(\mathrm{Br_2}\) has \(\mathrm{E^0} = 1.09\ \mathrm{V}\). Since \(1.36 > 1.09\), **\(\mathrm{Cl_2}\) is the stronger oxidising agent** — which is why chlorine displaces bromine from a bromide solution and not the reverse.

**b.** \(\mathrm{MnO_4^{\ominus}}\) has \(\mathrm{E^0} = 1.51\ \mathrm{V}\) and \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2\ominus}}\) has \(\mathrm{E^0} = 1.33\ \mathrm{V}\). Since \(1.51 > 1.33\), **\(\mathrm{MnO_4^{\ominus}}\) (permanganate) is the stronger oxidising agent.**

Both pairs of values agree with Table 6.1 of this chapter.

The chapter states the rule directly : a **large negative** value of \(\mathrm{E^0}\) means the redox couple is a strong reducing agent, because a large negative \(\mathrm{E^0}\) means a great tendency to give away electrons and form cations.

**a.** \(\mathrm{Li}\) has \(\mathrm{E^0} = -3.05\ \mathrm{V}\) and \(\mathrm{Mg}\) has \(\mathrm{E^0} = -2.36\ \mathrm{V}\). Since \(-3.05\) is the more negative, **\(\mathrm{Li}\) is the stronger reducing agent** — indeed it is the most negative entry in Table 6.1, and the chapter notes that the alkali metals are the strongest reducing agents in the table.

**b.** \(\mathrm{Zn}\) has \(\mathrm{E^0} = -0.76\ \mathrm{V}\) and \(\mathrm{Fe}\) has \(\mathrm{E^0} = -0.44\ \mathrm{V}\). Since \(-0.76\) is the more negative, **\(\mathrm{Zn}\) is the stronger reducing agent** — which is why zinc is used to protect iron from rusting.

[Textbook misprint: sub-item (d) is printed with the state symbol \((g)\) on \(\mathrm{Bi(OH)_3}\). Bismuth(III) hydroxide is an insoluble SOLID, and the book itself prints the same species as \(\mathrm{Bi(OH)_3(s)}\) in Q.4 B (b) on the same page. The stem is preserved as printed; the state symbol has no bearing on the balancing, which is unchanged.]

The chapter's oxidation number method is used throughout : balance every element except H and O, find the increase and decrease in oxidation number and make them equal, balance O with \(\mathrm{H_2O}\), balance H with \(\mathrm{H^{\oplus}}\), and — for a basic medium only — add as many \(\mathrm{OH^{\ominus}}\) to BOTH sides as there are \(\mathrm{H^{\oplus}}\), combining \(\mathrm{H^{\oplus}}\) and \(\mathrm{OH^{\ominus}}\) on the same side into water.

**a. \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2\ominus}(aq) + SO_3^{2\ominus}(aq) \longrightarrow Cr^{3\oplus}(aq) + SO_4^{2\ominus}(aq)}\) (acidic)**

Cr in \(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2\ominus}}\) is \(+6\) and becomes \(+3\) : decrease of 3 per Cr, so 6 per dichromate ion. S in \(\mathrm{SO_3^{2\ominus}}\) is \(+4\) and becomes \(+6\) : increase of 2 per S. To equalise, take 1 dichromate to 3 sulphite.

\(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2\ominus} + 3SO_3^{2\ominus} \longrightarrow 2Cr^{3\oplus} + 3SO_4^{2\ominus}}\)

O : 16 on the left, 12 on the right, so add \(\mathrm{4H_2O}\) on the right. H : 8 on the right, so add \(\mathrm{8H^{\oplus}}\) on the left (the medium is acidic, so no \(\mathrm{OH^{\ominus}}\) step).

\(\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2\ominus}(aq) + 3SO_3^{2\ominus}(aq) + 8H^{\oplus}(aq) \longrightarrow 2Cr^{3\oplus}(aq) + 3SO_4^{2\ominus}(aq) + 4H_2O}(l)\)

Check — atoms Cr 2/2, S 3/3, O 16/16, H 8/8; charge \((-2) + (-6) + (+8) = 0\) on the left and \((+6) + (-6) = 0\) on the right.

**b. \(\mathrm{MnO_4^{\ominus}(aq) + Br^{\ominus}(aq) \longrightarrow MnO_2(s) + BrO_3^{\ominus}(aq)}\) (basic)**

Mn is \(+7\) and becomes \(+4\) : decrease of 3. Br is \(-1\) and becomes \(+5\) : increase of 6. To equalise, take 2 permanganate to 1 bromide.

\(\mathrm{2MnO_4^{\ominus} + Br^{\ominus} \longrightarrow 2MnO_2 + BrO_3^{\ominus}}\)

O : 8 on the left, 7 on the right, so add \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) on the right; then add \(\mathrm{2H^{\oplus}}\) on the left for the 2 H. The medium is BASIC, so add \(\mathrm{2OH^{\ominus}}\) to both sides; the \(\mathrm{2H^{\oplus}}\) and \(\mathrm{2OH^{\ominus}}\) on the left give \(\mathrm{2H_2O}\), and one water cancels against the one on the right.

\(\mathrm{2MnO_4^{\ominus}(aq) + Br^{\ominus}(aq) + H_2O}(l) \mathrm{\longrightarrow 2MnO_2(s) + BrO_3^{\ominus}(aq) + 2OH^{\ominus}(aq)}\)

Check — atoms Mn 2/2, Br 1/1, O 9/9, H 2/2; charge \(-3\) on each side.

**c. \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4(aq) + C(s) \longrightarrow CO_2(g) + SO_2(g) + H_2O}(l)\) (acidic)**

C is \(0\) and becomes \(+4\) : increase of 4. S is \(+6\) and becomes \(+4\) : decrease of 2. To equalise, take 2 sulphuric acid to 1 carbon.

\(\mathrm{2H_2SO_4 + C \longrightarrow CO_2 + 2SO_2 + H_2O}\)

H : 4 on the left, so 2 water on the right; that also settles O at 8 on each side, and no \(\mathrm{H^{\oplus}}\) is needed.

\(\mathrm{2H_2SO_4(aq) + C(s) \longrightarrow CO_2(g) + 2SO_2(g) + 2H_2O}(l)\)

Check — atoms C 1/1, S 2/2, H 4/4, O 8/8; both sides neutral.

**d. \(\mathrm{Bi(OH)_3 + Sn(OH)_3^{\ominus}(aq) \longrightarrow Bi(s) + Sn(OH)_6^{2\ominus}(aq)}\) (basic)**

Bi is \(+3\) and becomes \(0\) : decrease of 3. Sn is \(+2\) and becomes \(+4\) : increase of 2. To equalise, take 2 bismuth to 3 tin.

\(\mathrm{2Bi(OH)_3 + 3Sn(OH)_3^{\ominus} \longrightarrow 2Bi + 3Sn(OH)_6^{2\ominus}}\)

The charge is \(-3\) on the left and \(-6\) on the right; the medium is basic, so make it up with \(\mathrm{3OH^{\ominus}}\) on the left, which simultaneously supplies the 3 O and 3 H the right-hand side is short of.

\(\mathrm{2Bi(OH)_3(s) + 3Sn(OH)_3^{\ominus}(aq) + 3OH^{\ominus}(aq) \longrightarrow 2Bi(s) + 3Sn(OH)_6^{2\ominus}(aq)}\)

Check — atoms Bi 2/2, Sn 3/3, O 18/18, H 18/18; charge \(-6\) on each side.

The chapter's ion electron (half reaction) method is used for both : split into an oxidation and a reduction half equation, balance each for O with \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) and for H with \(\mathrm{H^{\oplus}}\), balance the charges with electrons, multiply to equalise the electrons, add, and cancel.

**a. \(\mathrm{H_2C_2O_4(aq) + MnO_4^{\ominus}(aq) \longrightarrow CO_2(g) + Mn^{2\oplus}(aq)}\) (acidic)**

In \(\mathrm{H_2C_2O_4}\), \(2(+1) + 2x + 4(-2) = 0\) gives C \(= +3\); in \(\mathrm{CO_2}\), C is \(+4\). In \(\mathrm{MnO_4^{\ominus}}\), Mn is \(+7\); as \(\mathrm{Mn^{2\oplus}}\) it is \(+2\).

Oxidation half :

\(\mathrm{H_2C_2O_4(aq) \longrightarrow 2CO_2(g) + 2H^{\oplus}(aq) + 2e^{\ominus}}\)

Reduction half :

\(\mathrm{MnO_4^{\ominus}(aq) + 8H^{\oplus}(aq) + 5e^{\ominus} \longrightarrow Mn^{2\oplus}(aq) + 4H_2O}(l)\)

Multiply the oxidation half by 5 and the reduction half by 2 so that both carry 10 electrons, then add :

\(\mathrm{5H_2C_2O_4 + 2MnO_4^{\ominus} + 16H^{\oplus} \longrightarrow 10CO_2 + 10H^{\oplus} + 2Mn^{2\oplus} + 8H_2O}\)

Cancelling \(\mathrm{10H^{\oplus}}\) from both sides :

\(\mathrm{5H_2C_2O_4(aq) + 2MnO_4^{\ominus}(aq) + 6H^{\oplus}(aq) \longrightarrow 10CO_2(g) + 2Mn^{2\oplus}(aq) + 8H_2O}(l)\)

Check — atoms C 10/10, Mn 2/2, H 16/16, O 28/28; charge \((-2) + (+6) = +4\) on the left and \(2(+2) = +4\) on the right.

**b. \(\mathrm{Bi(OH)_3(s) + SnO_2^{2\ominus}(aq) \longrightarrow SnO_3^{2\ominus}(aq) + Bi(s)}\) (basic)**

Bi is \(+3\) in \(\mathrm{Bi(OH)_3}\) and \(0\) as the free metal. In \(\mathrm{SnO_2^{2\ominus}}\), \(x + 2(-2) = -2\) gives Sn \(= +2\); in \(\mathrm{SnO_3^{2\ominus}}\), \(x + 3(-2) = -2\) gives Sn \(= +4\).

Reduction half (3 electrons per Bi) :

\(\mathrm{Bi(OH)_3(s) + 3e^{\ominus} \longrightarrow Bi(s) + 3OH^{\ominus}(aq)}\)

Oxidation half (2 electrons per Sn ; in basic medium the extra O comes from \(\mathrm{OH^{\ominus}}\)) :

\(\mathrm{SnO_2^{2\ominus}(aq) + 2OH^{\ominus}(aq) \longrightarrow SnO_3^{2\ominus}(aq) + H_2O}(l) + \mathrm{2e^{\ominus}}\)

Multiply the reduction half by 2 and the oxidation half by 3 so that both carry 6 electrons, then add and cancel \(\mathrm{6OH^{\ominus}}\) from both sides :

\(\mathrm{2Bi(OH)_3(s) + 3SnO_2^{2\ominus}(aq) \longrightarrow 3SnO_3^{2\ominus}(aq) + 2Bi(s) + 3H_2O}(l)\)

Check — atoms Bi 2/2, Sn 3/3, O 12/12, H 6/6; charge \(-6\) on each side.

For each compound, apply the chapter's rules — Cl is \(-1\), O is \(-2\), H bonded to a non-metal is \(+1\) — and set the sum of all oxidation numbers equal to zero for a neutral compound or to the ionic charge for an ion. Then write the value as a Roman numeral in parentheses after the underlined element's symbol.

| Compound | Working | Oxidation number | Stock notation |
|---|---|---|---|
| \(\underline{\mathrm{Au}}\mathrm{Cl_3}\) | \(x + 3(-1) = 0\) | \(+3\) | \(\mathrm{Au(III)Cl_3}\) |
| \(\underline{\mathrm{Sn}}\mathrm{Cl_2}\) | \(x + 2(-1) = 0\) | \(+2\) | \(\mathrm{Sn(II)Cl_2}\) |
| \(\underline{\mathrm{V}}_2\mathrm{O_7^{4\ominus}}\) | \(2x + 7(-2) = -4\) | \(+5\) | \(\mathrm{V(V)_2O_7^{4\ominus}}\) |
| \(\underline{\mathrm{Pt}}\mathrm{Cl_6^{2\ominus}}\) | \(x + 6(-1) = -2\) | \(+4\) | \(\mathrm{Pt(IV)Cl_6^{2\ominus}}\) |
| \(\mathrm{H_3}\underline{\mathrm{As}}\mathrm{O_3}\) | \(3(+1) + x + 3(-2) = 0\) | \(+3\) | \(\mathrm{H_3As(III)O_3}\) |

Note that the last two entries are ions, not neutral molecules, so their oxidation numbers sum to the ionic charge (\(-4\) and \(-2\)) rather than to zero — rule 7 rather than rule 6.
